title: 2 Samuel 3:31–39
context: David orders Joab and all the people to tear their clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner, and he himself follows the bier. At Abner’s grave in Hebron the king weeps aloud and laments that Abner died as a fool dies, not bound or fettered but fallen before wicked men. David refuses to eat until sundown, and the people take notice and are pleased. All Israel comes to understand that the king had no part in Abner’s death. David tells his servants that a prince and a great man has fallen, confesses that he is weak though anointed while the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him, and leaves their punishment to the LORD. Both traditions read this as a sober picture of public grief, political integrity, and the limits of a king’s power.

verses.text: David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, “Tear your clothes, and clothe yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn in front of Abner.” King David followed the bier.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David requires Joab himself to mourn publicly before Abner. Making the killer join the mourning is a pointed public act, and David’s following the bier shows the king personally honoring the man his commander killed, which signals his real grief and disapproval.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s command to mourn and his presence at the bier are acts of public integrity. Both traditions agree that David is distancing himself from the murder in the clearest possible way, and that his mourning is presented as both genuine and politically important.

verses.text: They buried Abner in Hebron; and the king lifted up his voice and wept at Abner’s grave; and all the people wept.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Abner is buried in Hebron, and the king lifts up his voice and weeps at his grave, with all the people weeping too. The shared grief shows the community gathered around the king, and David’s tears express sincere sorrow for a former enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that David weeps for a man who had fought against him, which reflects a generous spirit toward an opponent. Both traditions agree that the scene presents David’s grief as authentic, and that the people’s response shows that they accept his sincerity.

verses.text: The king lamented for Abner, and said, “Should Abner die as a fool dies?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David laments by asking whether Abner should die as a fool dies. In the wisdom tradition, a fool is someone morally careless whose end is shameful; David’s question suggests that Abner, a capable man, did not deserve such an ignominious death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s lament mourns the manner of Abner’s death as much as the death itself. Both traditions agree that the lament honors Abner’s stature while drawing attention to the injustice of how he died, through treachery rather than in open battle.

verses.text: Your hands weren’t bound, and your feet weren’t put into fetters. As a man falls before the children of iniquity, so you fell.” All the people wept again over him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that David says Abner’s hands were not bound and his feet not fettered, meaning he was neither a prisoner nor a condemned man, yet he fell before the children of iniquity. The lament names the killers’ act as wicked, though without naming them directly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that David’s lament implicitly condemns Joab and Abishai by calling the deed the work of wicked men. Both traditions agree that the people weeping again shows how deeply the lament struck them, and that David’s words publicly place the guilt where it belongs.

verses.text: All the people came to urge David to eat bread while it was yet day; but David swore, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if I taste bread or anything else, until the sun goes down.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that David swears not to eat until sundown despite the people urging him. His fast is a visible sign of mourning, and the oath demonstrates that his grief is not a show for a moment but a sustained response throughout the day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that fasting accompanies mourning elsewhere in Scripture, as David and his men did for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:12). Both traditions agree that David’s refusal of food shows both personal sorrow and a public commitment that the people could see.

verses.text: All the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as whatever the king did pleased all the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the people took notice and were pleased, and that whatever the king did pleased them. This reflects David’s standing with the people and the trust he has earned, which is essential for the unity of the kingdom he is building.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the people’s approval is a sign that David’s integrity is recognized. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the political importance of David’s conduct, as his response to Abner’s death strengthens rather than weakens the people’s confidence in him.

verses.text: So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it was not of the king to kill Abner the son of Ner.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that all the people and all Israel understood that it was not the king’s doing to kill Abner. The verse states the outcome the narrator has been building toward: David’s innocence is publicly recognized, which removes a serious obstacle to the union of the tribes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Israel’s understanding is central to the narrative’s purpose. Both traditions agree that the account is designed to show that David came to the throne without murdering his rivals, and that his reputation for justice is preserved even amid violence he did not order.

verses.text: The king said to his servants, “Don’t you know that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that David calls Abner a prince and a great man fallen in Israel. David speaks generously of a former opponent, honoring his stature and recognizing his loss to the nation, which models a kind of magnanimity toward rivals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note David’s honoring of Abner and his recognition of what Israel has lost. Both traditions agree that David’s words do not erase Abner’s earlier opposition but show that David valued him as a leader whose death was a real loss to the people.

verses.text: I am weak today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me. May the LORD reward the evildoer according to his wickedness.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that David confesses that he is weak, though anointed king, and that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him. His admission is honest about the limits of his power, and he entrusts justice to the LORD, asking that the evildoer be repaid according to his wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s anointing does not give him unlimited control over his own commanders, and he leaves vengeance to the LORD. Both traditions agree that the verse shows David’s honesty and his reliance on God for justice, while also leaving readers aware that Joab’s crime remains unpunished for now.
